patient.name: Leah Okafor
patient.complaint: Vulval itch and thick white discharge, her fourth episode this year, plus a sore white tongue
background: Asthma on beclometasone inhaler, no spacer
Amoxicillin for a chest infection 10 days ago
Thirsty and passing urine more often lately

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with itchy cottage-cheese discharge and no odour (vaginal), white plaques that scrape off (oral), or satellite lesions in a skin fold; odynophagia in HIV means oesophageal candidiasis.

points: Leah, 34: **vulval itch** and soreness for 4 days.
Discharge is **thick, white, like cottage cheese**.
**No fishy smell.** Fourth episode this year.

steps.lead: Leah's amoxicillin killed her protective flora, letting **Candida albicans** overgrow.

points: Her tongue is sore; she uses her **steroid inhaler without a spacer**.
White plaques on tongue and palate **scrape off** to a red base.
Vulva red and swollen; white curd-like discharge.

steps.lead: Leah has two of the three classic sites: **vaginal** (cottage cheese, no smell, OCP) and **oral** (plaques that scrape off, inhaled steroid).

visual.title: Vaginal pH
visual.label: Leah 4.2
visual.caption: Candida leaves the pH normal. A raised pH points to BV or trichomonas.

steps.q: Leah's discharge has no smell and her pH is normal. Which is the most likely cause?
steps.r: Itchy, thick white, odourless discharge with a normal pH is **vulvovaginal candidiasis**.

steps.lead: Four episodes in a year is **recurrent** thrush, and Leah is thirsty: check **HbA1c** to exclude diabetes.
If Leah had **dysphagia and painful swallowing** with advanced HIV, she would have **oesophageal candidiasis**, an AIDS-defining illness.
In a severely immunocompromised patient (neutropenia, ICU, central lines), Candida can enter the blood: **systemic candidiasis**.

steps.text: **Oral hairy leukoplakia** (EBV, in HIV) is white on the side of the tongue but does **not scrape off**. Candida plaques do.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where the answer is usually none (clinical), HbA1c for recurrent thrush, or microscopy for budding yeast when the picture is atypical.

steps.q: Leah's thrush looks classic. What confirms the diagnosis today?
steps.r: Candidiasis is usually a **clinical diagnosis**; swab only if the picture is not typical.

steps.lead: Leah's classic appearance is enough. If in doubt, microscopy shows **budding yeast** (with pseudohyphae).
Because Leah's thrush is **recurrent**, she needs an **HbA1c**; a swab is only needed if the symptoms are not clearly thrush.

steps.title: Leah's bloods
steps.text: An HbA1c of 61 diagnoses **type 2 diabetes**: glucose-rich secretions feed Candida.

visual.title: Leah's HbA1c
visual.label: Leah 61
visual.caption: 48 mmol/mol or above diagnoses diabetes. Untreated diabetes is a classic driver of recurrent thrush.

steps.text: Recurrent thrush is **four or more episodes a year**. The question line will often want **HbA1c**, not another swab.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': oral fluconazole 150 mg single dose for vaginal thrush, clotrimazole pessary if pregnant, miconazole oral gel for oral thrush, topical azole for skin.

steps.title: Choosing the antifungal by site
nodes: Vaginal, not pregnant: fluconazole 150 mg PO once
Oral: miconazole oral gel (nystatin if not)
Skin folds: topical clotrimazole or miconazole
steps.caption: Site and pregnancy decide the drug.

steps.lead: Leah's oral thrush gets **miconazole oral gel**. A single episode of vaginal thrush would be **fluconazole 150 mg PO once**.

steps.q: If Leah were 20 weeks pregnant with the same vaginal symptoms, what would you give?
steps.r: Avoid oral azoles in pregnancy: use an **intravaginal clotrimazole** pessary.

steps.lead: Leah's vaginal thrush is **recurrent**, so she gets **3 doses of oral fluconazole 150 mg**. Nystatin suspension is the oral thrush alternative.
To stop her oral thrush coming back, Leah should **use a spacer** and **rinse her mouth** after her steroid inhaler.

visual.title: Leah's thrush episodes per 6 months
visual.caption: Diabetes control, the fluconazole induction course and a spacer stopped the recurrences.

steps.text: Do not stop Leah's inhaled steroid for oral thrush: her asthma needs it. Fix the **technique**: spacer and mouth rinse.
Thrush is **not** a sexually transmitted infection: partners do not need routine treatment.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why antibiotics, steroids, diabetes or HIV let Candida overgrow, why it likes warm moist sites, and how azoles work.

steps.lead: Candida is normal flora in Leah's mouth and vagina. **Amoxicillin** removed the competing bacteria; diabetes added fuel.
Warm, moist places, Leah's mouth and vagina, and skin folds in others, let Candida thrive.
Leah's inhaled steroid, landing on her tongue without a spacer, **suppresses local immunity** in the oropharynx.
Oesophageal spread needs a **profound loss of cell-mediated immunity**, which is why it defines AIDS.

visual.title: CD4 count and candidiasis
visual.label: Example: 120
visual.caption: The lower the CD4 count, the deeper Candida goes: mouth first, then oesophagus.

steps.title: How azoles kill Candida
steps.caption: Humans use cholesterol, not ergosterol, so the target is fungus-specific.

steps.lead: Leah's fluconazole and miconazole both block **ergosterol synthesis**.

steps.text: Azoles inhibit **CYP450**, so fluconazole and miconazole gel can raise **warfarin** and statin levels. Always check the drug chart.

o: Thick white, cottage cheese, no odour

mcq.q: What distinguishes oral candida plaques from leukoplakia?

mcq.r: Azoles block **ergosterol synthesis**; polyenes bind ergosterol.

o: Destruction of normal oral flora by the inhaler
Local immunosuppression of the oropharynx by corticosteroid
Low CD4 count from HIV infection
Raised salivary glucose from steroid-induced diabetes

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

practice.stem: A 45 year old man with asthma uses a fluticasone inhaler twice daily without a spacer. He has a 2 week history of a sore mouth and altered taste. There are creamy white plaques on his tongue and soft palate that scrape off, leaving a red, raw surface. His temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 72 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: White plaques that scrape off to a red base in an inhaled steroid user are oral candidiasis. Leukoplakia and lichen planus do not scrape off.

clues: scrape off, leaving a red, raw surface
steps.x: Inhaled steroid, no spacer, plaques that scrape off.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Painful round ulcers with a yellow base; not plaques.

practice.stem:
A 39 year old man with HIV who stopped his antiretrovirals a year ago has a 3 week history of pain on swallowing and food sticking behind his sternum. He has white plaques on his tongue. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.

Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Odynophagia and dysphagia with oral thrush and a CD4 below 200 is oesophageal candidiasis, an AIDS-defining illness.

Odynophagia, dysphagia, oral thrush, CD4 below 200.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman with obesity and type 2 diabetes has a 2 week history of an itchy, sore rash under both breasts. The skin is bright red and moist, with small separate red papules and pustules beyond the main edge. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A moist red rash in a skin fold with satellite papules and pustules in a diabetic is cutaneous candidiasis. Inverse psoriasis has no satellite lesions.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Brown, dry, scaly patches; fluoresces coral red; no satellites.
Well-demarcated, shiny red plaques without satellite lesions.
Greasy scale on the scalp, face and chest.
Annular scaly ring with central clearing, usually not in moist folds.

steps.x: **A. Cutaneous candidiasis.** Satellite lesions are the clue.

glossary.Candidiasis: Infection caused by Candida yeasts, usually Candida albicans.
glossary.Candida albicans: The commonest Candida yeast; normal flora of mouth, gut and vagina.
glossary.Thrush: Common name for oral or vaginal candidiasis.
glossary.Normal flora: Microbes that live harmlessly on the body and keep pathogens in check.
glossary.Budding yeast: Yeast cells reproducing by small outgrowths, seen on microscopy in candidiasis.
glossary.Pseudohyphae: Chains of elongated yeast cells, typical of Candida on microscopy.
glossary.Satellite lesions: Small separate red spots beyond the main edge of a rash; classic for cutaneous candidiasis.
glossary.Intertrigo: Inflammation of skin folds from friction and moisture, often infected by Candida.
glossary.AIDS-defining illness: An infection or cancer that signals advanced HIV with severe immune loss.
glossary.CD4 count: Number of helper T cells; below 200 cells/µL defines AIDS.
glossary.Cell-mediated immunity: T-cell driven immunity that controls fungi, viruses and intracellular organisms.
glossary.Systemic candidiasis: Candida in the blood or organs, in severely immunocompromised patients.
glossary.HbA1c: Glycated haemoglobin, showing average glucose over about 3 months; 48 mmol/mol or above means diabetes.
glossary.OCP: Oral contraceptive pill, a risk factor for vaginal thrush.
glossary.ICS: Inhaled corticosteroid, used in asthma and COPD; causes oral thrush.
glossary.Spacer: A chamber attached to an inhaler that reduces drug deposited in the mouth.
glossary.Fluconazole: Oral azole antifungal; 150 mg single dose treats vaginal thrush.
glossary.Clotrimazole: Topical or vaginal azole antifungal; the pessary is used in pregnancy.
glossary.Miconazole: Azole antifungal; oral gel is first line for oral thrush.
glossary.Nystatin: Polyene antifungal suspension used for oral thrush; not absorbed from the gut.
glossary.Azole: Antifungal class that blocks ergosterol synthesis.
glossary.Ergosterol: The sterol in fungal cell membranes, equivalent to cholesterol in human cells.
glossary.Lanosterol 14α-demethylase: Fungal CYP450 enzyme making ergosterol; the target of azoles.
glossary.Pessary: A medicated tablet inserted into the vagina.
glossary.Bacterial vaginosis: Overgrowth of anaerobes such as Gardnerella, giving thin fishy discharge and raised pH.
glossary.Trichomonas vaginalis: Sexually transmitted protozoan causing frothy, offensive yellow-green discharge.
glossary.Oral hairy leukoplakia: EBV-related white ridges on the side of the tongue in HIV; does not scrape off.
glossary.Leukoplakia: A white oral patch that cannot be scraped off; potentially premalignant.
glossary.Erythrasma: Corynebacterium skin-fold infection; brown scaly patches that fluoresce coral red under Wood's lamp.
